# glee54math — Own-Platform Analysis

*Generated by an agent reading the codebase at `inventory-tracking/pel-sr-ims` (App.tsx, routes/, components/student_portal, components/parent_portal, components/student_progress_dashboard, pages/math-levels, pages/english-levels, utils/homeworkPrediction.ts, utils/progressService.ts, utils/authService.ts, utils/firebase.ts, and the `.claude/agents/math-lab-builder.md` + `.claude/skills/build-math-lab/SKILL.md` design docs). This is the baseline against which the 20 platform profiles in `platform-profiles.md` are compared.*

## Product / UX

The platform splits cleanly into three experiences gated by role in AppRoutes.tsx/ProtectedRoutes.tsx: an operational "App" for admin/worker staff (inventory + homework assignment), a parent dashboard, and a student portal. Onboarding is asymmetric — parents sign up with email/Google and link children seemingly via manual staff help (ParentDashboard shows "contact Mr. Lee" when no children are linked), while students skip individual accounts entirely: they enter a single shared 4-digit PIN ("1234" in StudentLogin.tsx) and then pick their own name from a dropdown listing every enrolled student. This is extremely low-friction for young kids but has no onboarding tutorial of any kind. The student dashboard (StudentDashboard.tsx) composes level-status cards, a collapsible Homework Queue sorted by date, a Practice Problems entry point, a Supplemental Level Browser that only exposes levels up to the student's current level (grouped by grade band), and a locked "What's Next" card. Content itself is not generic multiple-choice: each grade level is a hand-built interactive React "lab" with Explore / Check-for-Understanding / Practice / Test stages (per math-lab-builder.md), which is richer than most quiz-style ed-tech but means content creation is bespoke engineering rather than CMS-driven authoring. The UI is Tailwind-based and responsive at the breakpoint level, but there is no evidence of a dedicated mobile app, offline mode, or PWA packaging — it is web-only. Accessibility is largely unaddressed: status is frequently color-only (green/red/yellow badges) without accompanying iconography beyond text, and some controls are bare emoji buttons ("🔄", "👁️") with no visible aria-label.

## Engagement Mechanics

The strongest engagement work is pedagogical rather than cosmetic. `useModuleProgress`'s shared `isMastered`/`starCount` logic awards stars proportional to the fraction of a unit's "required buckets" (distinct problem scenario-classes) actually covered, capping below full mastery until every bucket is hit and only then jumping to the max — rewarding genuine breadth of skill over grinding the easy case repeatedly. Every unit can carry a `requiresIntro` Check-for-Understanding gate with fixed questions engineered to hit vocabulary, commonly-conflated concepts, and true/false generalizations before full Practice unlocks, and a `reintroEverySolved` flag periodically re-surfaces the guided walkthrough for facts meant to be memorized long-term — a real, codified spaced-retention mechanic (recognized internally as still incomplete, per the "retention/pacing/scaffolding-fade gaps" follow-up noted elsewhere). `homeworkPrediction.ts` adds adaptive pacing by inferring Advance/Reinforce/Repeat suggestions from a student's actual assignment history, though this is staff-facing rather than a student-visible adaptive path. Student-facing gamification is otherwise light: a locked "What's Next" card behind a second hardcoded PIN and a browsable list of already-unlocked supplemental levels are the extent of it — there are no streaks, points, badges, leaderboards, or daily-goal nudges. There are also no community or social features whatsoever, and no visible re-engagement mechanism such as email/push reminders for lapsed students.

## Business Model

No pricing, billing, subscription, payment-processor, or certificate/credentialing code exists anywhere in the reviewed surface, and there is no self-serve acquisition funnel. Every error/empty state that would normally be a monetization or support touchpoint instead names a person directly — "contact Mr. Lee at pelsanramon@gmail.com" — strongly suggesting this is the internal software for a single in-person tutoring center (inventory tracking for physical worksheet packets plus a digital companion portal) rather than a direct-to-consumer SaaS product. Parent registration exists and defaults new sign-ups to a "parent" role, but linking a child to that parent account appears to require manual/admin intervention, consistent with human-mediated enrollment and billing happening entirely outside the app.

## Trust & Social Proof

There are no testimonials, reviews, or third-party social-proof elements anywhere in the product — trust is built entirely through the named human contact rather than in-app credibility signals. More materially, the access-control model has real gaps for a product that surfaces per-child academic history: StudentLogin.tsx gates the entire student portal behind one shared 4-digit PIN common to all students, after which anyone holding that PIN can select and view/act as *any* enrolled student's name from a dropdown — there is no per-student credential. WhatsNextCard.tsx layers a second hardcoded PIN ("3188") shipped directly in the client bundle, which functions only as a UX speed-bump, not a security boundary. No `firestore.rules` file was found anywhere in the repository, so the actual server-side authorization policy protecting Firestore data cannot be verified from the codebase. These are reasonable trade-offs for low-friction access by young children in a trusted, in-person-center context, but are not defensible as access control if the platform is ever opened to a broader, less-trusted audience.

## Technical Design

The stack is a standard modern SPA: React + TypeScript on Vite, Tailwind, react-router-dom, and Firebase (Firestore + Auth) as the only backend — no custom server/API layer. The progress-tracking engine (progressService.ts) is the most sophisticated part of the system: `toDate()` normalizes Firestore Timestamps/ISO strings/numbers/Date objects at every boundary, and `buildStudentProgress` reconciles manually-entered "historical" level data against inferred data from the append-only `hwkAssigned` log, cascading start/end dates across level transitions. This shows real engineering investment in surviving messy legacy data, but the function is very long, duplicates nearly identical logic between the Math and English branches, and still carries numerous debug `console.log` calls in production code. Real-time behavior is inconsistent: the admin inventory view uses a live Firestore `onSnapshot` listener, while student/parent progress is fetched once and only refreshed via an explicit "Refresh Progress" button. The most distinctive technical asset is the content-authoring system: curriculum units are built against a typed `Unit`/`Problem`/`Step` engine in `shared/engine` and `shared/diagrams`, with mastery math centralized in one hook, and an explicit two-stage pipeline — a `build-math-lab` planning skill handing off to a `math-lab-builder` subagent — governed by a living style guide and a mandatory verification checklist (tsc/eslint/vite build, Monte Carlo trials of generators, manual browser smoke tests). Integrations are limited to Firebase Auth; no analytics SDK, email/SMS provider, payment processor, or LMS/SIS integration is present, and progress analytics are limited to pass/fail and pages-completed counts rather than per-question timing or attempt-level telemetry.

## Support Model

Support is entirely human and manual: every failure or empty state routes back to one named person's personal email address rather than any in-app help center, chat widget, ticketing system, or FAQ. There is no community surface in the product, so there is nothing to moderate. Content/curriculum update cadence, however, is unusually well-structured for an internal tool: new levels and units are produced through the codified `build-math-lab`/`math-lab-builder` pipeline, with conventions and open work tracked in living documents (`MATH_TSX_STYLE_GUIDE.txt`, `VISUAL_COMPONENT_TODO.txt`) — effectively a documented internal content-ops workflow, even though none of it is customer-facing.

## Summary — Pros

- Bucket-coverage-weighted mastery/star system rewards genuine breadth of skill, not just repetition volume
- Mandatory Check-for-Understanding gates target vocabulary, commonly-conflated concepts, and generalizations before full practice unlocks
- `reintroEverySolved` flag gives a codified spaced-retention mechanic for facts meant to be memorized long-term
- Staff-facing homework-prediction engine (Advance/Reinforce/Repeat) personalizes next assignments from real per-student history
- Rich hand-built Explore→CFU→Practice→Test→Module-Test labs per level, well beyond generic multiple-choice practice
- Parent portal shows real per-child level timelines and estimated completion dates, not just a percent-complete bar
- PIN-based student login removes friction appropriate for young children who can't manage full credentials
- Unusually mature internal content-authoring system: typed shared engine/diagram library, documented conventions, and an automated build-and-verify pipeline for new curriculum
- Progress-reconciliation logic thoughtfully merges manually entered historical data with log-inferred data to survive messy legacy records

## Summary — Cons

- Shared 4-digit student PIN plus a second hardcoded client-side PIN are not real access control — any holder can view or act as any other enrolled student
- No `firestore.rules` found in the repo, so server-side data-access enforcement cannot be verified from code
- No streaks, badges, leaderboards, or daily-goal/re-engagement notifications — gamification stops at stars and a single locked card
- No community or peer/social features at all (no classmates, forums, or shared activity)
- No visible pricing, billing, or self-serve signup/account-linking funnel — enrollment depends on emailing a named staff member
- Core `buildStudentProgress` logic is very long, nearly duplicated between Math and English branches, and still ships debug `console.log` calls
- No accessibility affordances evident (aria-labels, alt text, keyboard navigation); some status cues rely on color or bare emoji alone
- Real-time sync is inconsistent: admin inventory updates live via `onSnapshot`, but student/parent progress only refreshes on manual action
- Analytics are limited to pass/fail and page counts, with no per-question timing or attempt-level data for staff to diagnose struggle points
- No testimonials, reviews, or any trust/social-proof elements inside the product itself
